items.title: Printing iPhone Photos Cheaply using an Amazon Kids Instant Print Camera
items.summary: If you’ve got one of these little instant print cameras and you…
items.content_html:
If you’ve got one of these little instant print cameras and you want to get your iPhone photos onto it, the process is surprisingly straightforward once you know the trick.

I played around with a couple of test photos and quickly realized the camera is picky about file format. Here’s what it wants:

  • Filename: follow the PICT####.jpg naming convention.
  • Dimensions: fixed at 3840 × 2160 pixels.
  • Color Depth: 24-bit.
  • DPI: 96 × 96.

Once I figured that out, I built a simple, repeatable flow. I’m on Windows, but Mac folks should be able to find comparable apps to get the same result.

My Workflow

  1. Take the photo on iPhone.
  2. Transfer to PC with SimpleTransfer, converting from HEIC to JPG.
  3. Fix orientation (if needed): if it’s vertical, rotate to landscape—otherwise the camera prints it tiny.
  4. Insert the SD card: pull it from the camera and plug it into the computer. (alternatively just plug in the camera and point the output folder to the SD Card).
  5. Batch convert with FastStone:
    • Rename files to match PICT####.jpg.
    • Crop/resize to 3840 × 2160.
    • Start numbering at the next available photo number (last photo number on the card + 1).
  6. Output directly to the SD card in the correct format and size.
  7. Eject & print: safely remove the card, pop it back in the camera, open Playback, pick the photo, and hit Print.

That’s it. Do it once or twice and it’s second nature. If you’ve been banging your head trying to get iPhone photos to print on this little camera, this should save you the headache.

You can also use it to print cute little messages for your kids lunches if you don't have a printer available. I used Chatgpt to generate the background and embedded my message inside it.

items.title: My hunt for the perfect souvenir travel camera
items.summary: I recently went on a hiking trip to Scottsdale, AZ with friends…
items.content_html:
I recently went on a hiking trip to Scottsdale, AZ with friends and had a blast. One friend brought an Instax camera, and everyone got to take home a little souvenir. That lit a bulb for me.

When I got home I decided I wanted a new way to capture the essence of trips. I used to buy magnets; now I want to slap a magnetic backing on a small photo and stick it on my metal door. Simple, personal, and visible.

After a little research, I realized I basically needed three things:

  • A camera or printer I can take on trips to print photos of the experience.
  • Something my two sons can operate—so the memories can be from their eyes. Because of kid factor, I didn’t want to spend a lot (high breakage risk).
  • If it’s a camera, it should connect to my iPhone via Bluetooth or a memory card so I can print my own photos later. A portable printer would also solve this.

The camera my friend had ($93)

I started with the same camera my friend used. I almost bought it, but kept digging.

Pros: Price isn’t terrible; cute, kid-friendly design.

Cons: No SD card storage, so printing external photos isn’t really an option. Film is pricey—about $16 for 20 shots. Quality is great, but that price pushes it into “special occasions only.”

A higher-end camera version ($159)

More expensive, but it does let you print from your phone. Progress.

Pros: Better photo quality, and you can store to an SD card.

Cons: The price makes me nervous with two little boys who love pressing every button. Film cost is still the same story.

The highest-end camera option ($349)

At this point I was just exploring the “nice someday” tier. I love the aesthetic and the quality.

Pros: Excellent photo quality; Bluetooth printing.

Cons: Expensive camera plus expensive film. Not kid-proof enough for me right now.

A portable printer ($99)

By now I was leaning printer. The boys already have a cheap dino camera, and I’ve got my iPhone—no need to reinvent the wheel. It was pricier than I wanted (was hoping for ~$50), but it checked the boxes.

Pros: Portable, easy to use with multiple devices, just get photos onto my phone and print.

Cons: Reviews were mixed but mostly positive. Film/sheets still add up.

The version I actually bought ($31)

Then I found this little camera. It hit the sweet spot: let the kids take the photos, and I could still print my own later.

Pros: Cheap rolls of black-and-white thermal paper, kid-friendly design. I wasn’t 100% sure I could print from my phone or PC at first, but after getting it I figured out a simple hack. You can see exactly how to do it in this post.

Cons: It’s cheap, so photo and print quality are low (and B&W only). But that’s fine for my goal: quick, gratitude-triggering souvenirs—not gallery pieces.

Now that I know I can print external photos on this camera, I’m genuinely happy with the purchase. It does exactly what I wanted for these little trip souvenirs.

items.title: Storms, Robots, and Rooftops: A New York Story
items.summary: The trip started like most bad trips do: with weather, delays, and…
items.content_html:
The trip started like most bad trips do: with weather, delays, and the slow grind of airport bureaucracy. Tucson to Denver was supposed to be a short hop. Instead, we tangoed with a storm that dropped us in Wichita for refueling, then limped back to Denver hours too late. By then, my connection to New York had already gone without me.

The airline gave me a hotel voucher, a meal voucher, the usual sympathy packet of corporate apology. Four hours in a bed that still smelled faintly of the last guy’s deodorant, then back on a plane at dawn. By the time I finally hit New York, I was running on bad sleep and caffeine.

The hotel near Chelsea had a view worth a moment’s pause: the Empire State building looming like a weary old heavyweight, streets pulsing below with the kind of energy only New York manages at 8 a.m. I dropped my bag, inhaled the city grit, and walked to the office.

Inside, chaos and creativity. Max—my colleague—was hunched over a robot that would later be kicked around for a shoot. Cookies materialized from somewhere (New York has a way of producing perfect little indulgences out of thin air), and the fridge was stocked like we were actually going to need hydration for whatever came next.

By late afternoon, we were on a rooftop in the East Village with the CEO. One of those rare, candid moments where leadership pulls back the curtain. A circle of us, tossing questions like darts, him answering with surprising directness. 

Then came the party. My colleague Liam and I presented the new features of n8n to a room of creators, engineers, and flowgrammers. Afterward, the real show began: conversations, questions, the cocktail party current of New York’s tech underground. By the time I made it to the bar, it was already shut down. Maybe that was for the best!

The next morning, breakfast with Lucas, another colleague, before heading into a recording studio. We interviewed a customer about how they used the platform. No marketing fluff, just real talk about work, automation, and how people bend tools to their will.

Then came the main event: The Agentic Arena. Esports meets reality show, but instead of fragging each other in Halo, contestants built workflows in real time for a shot at ten grand. It went on for a while, 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.,but watching the tension build, the crowd lean in, it was its own kind of spectacle. Afterward: pizza, networking, more conversations. The New York way.

Dinner that night was with creators, the kind of dinner where you leave with more questions than answers, but also a strange sense of community. I met Nate Herk, the king of n8n on YouTube by views. I ended the night with cheesecake from a bakery (souvenir sugar) and a tres leches cake that I probably didn’t need but couldn’t resist.

The flight home was mercifully uneventful. No storms, no diversions, no deodorant-scented hotel layovers.

New York is never easy. It’s a fight every step of the way, against weather, crowds, your own exhaustion. But it’s worth it. Every time.

items.title: Work Trip to San Fransisco California
items.summary: Success measured by output. We got a lot done. A (mostly) working…
items.content_html:
Success measured by output. We got a lot done. A (mostly) working UI and full database schema ready to go. In that time we spent a lot of time at the Salesforce tower. A really pretty building that we had the priviledge to work there. 

Day 1: Hitting the ground running. 

I landed and pretty quickly went to the office to work with Dylan. On a steady diet of coffee, we pumped out a beautiful website UI and database scheme that worked with n8n to provide a powerful backend, and a useful front end. I can't wait to demo it!

Day 2: Work and Prep for Meetup

It was really difficult to stop working on the Content Creators dashboard and shift gears to prepping for the community meetup, but we did, and it went really well. A lot of the things that were issues before, like having too many speakers were fixed by having less speakers and more Q&A time. I think it really made the audience feel involved.

Day 3 - Work from Hotel Lobby Day

The last day was pretty uneventful. I hung out in hotel lobby and worked on various projects and had a few meetings. 

Also, lesson learned, a USB C fast charger will trickle charge a Macbook Pro.

items.title: New York in August: Work, Bagels, and a Bit of Adventure
items.summary: I just wrapped up a quick solo work trip to New York…
items.content_html:
I just wrapped up a quick solo work trip to New York City—cool weather, a packed schedule, and just enough downtime to explore the city in my own way.

✈ Getting There (Eventually)

This trip started with a hiccup: what should have been a Wednesday night arrival turned into a bleary-eyed 4 a.m. Thursday check-in, thanks to a United Airlines outage. On the bright side, my Houston leg was in first class, which softened the blow.

🏨 Staying in the Flatiron

I stayed at the Freehand Hotel in the Flatiron District. The place had character—modern design, good location—but did try to sneak in an extra fee. Luckily, my company covered it.

☕ Bagels & Pizza (Because New York)

My first morning, I walked to our NYC office, grabbing a breakfast bagel from Gramercy Bagels along the way. It was exactly what you want from a New York bagel—chewy, fresh, and satisfying.

Dinner highlights included East Village Pizza (classic NYC slice vibes) and Tenjou for ramen, which came with a surprise: the noodles and broth were served separately. It took me a moment to figure out the hidden broth compartment, but once I did, it was pure comfort food.

💼 Work That Didn’t Feel Like Work

The NYC office is less “cubicles and fluorescent lights” and more “incubator coworking space,” which made it a great spot for filming some content. I spent time chatting with my coworkers, especially Eunice and Zarif, and enjoyed swapping stories over pizza one night.

The main reason for the trip was to present at a customer training session. Initially, my section of the demo was going to be cut, but the client ended up giving us the final hour—a slot no other vendor (including Google Firebase or Microsoft Power Automate) received.

During the session, the client champion invited attendees to stick around for a deeper dive with me. Seven people stayed, and three of them were so engaged that what was supposed to be 30 minutes turned into a full hour. I showed three demos:

  • Star Wars workflow
  • Request Router
  • Call Forge for AI prompt management

The LinkedIn request router especially caught their attention, they were already imagining how to repurpose it for email.

🎥 Behind the Scenes

After the demo, I headed back to the office with Liam (a newer teammate who’s sharp and detail-oriented) to film a benchmarking short. Later, I walked back to the hotel in the cool NYC air—a small, refreshing moment in a packed trip.

🛍 Souvenirs & Sights

One highlight was The Friends Experience, where I picked up some souvenirs. I also took some time to just sit on a park bench, with two strangers, and watch the city go by. There was something so peaceful about just sitting there, no place to go or be, and just take in the sounds and sights.

🧠 Reflections

What I loved:

  • The energy of presenting and seeing people excited about the demos
  • Great food (those bagels…)
  • Making progress on big work projects even in between events
  • Feeling safe and relaxed walking alone at night

What I didn’t love:

  • That unnecessary hotel fee attempt
  • That there weren’t more n8n employees to interact with.

Overall, the trip was the perfect mix of productive and restorative. I left feeling inspired, connected to my team, and reminded why I love the energy of New York, especially when I can blend work with little slices of everyday city life.

items.title: Berlin, Germany - Company Meetup IRL
items.summary: Day 1 in Berlin – Tuesday I arrived late Tuesday and wasn’t…
items.content_html:
Day 1 in Berlin – Tuesday

I arrived late Tuesday and wasn’t sure what to do with my first evening in the city. I wandered into a small convenience store and picked up a bottle of German wine.

Before enjoying it back at my place, I stopped at a kebab shop for a kebab burger.

It was decent and filling. Afterward, I had a craving for something sweet, so I visited a local bakery and picked up a chocolate croissant to pair with the wine.

The croissant was a little on the stale side, but still tasty. The wine was excellent.

I called it an early night to rest up for the days ahead.

Day 2 in Berlin – Wednesday

A Busy Day in Berlin

I woke up around 9 AM, feeling surprisingly rested. Breakfast at the hotel was simple but satisfying—enough to fuel up for the long day ahead. After a quick shower, I got ready and called an Uber to the company hotel, where I dropped off my luggage before heading out for a walk.


View from my hotel room

The crisp Berlin air was refreshing, and I took advantage of the morning light to snap some photos during my walk. After looping back to the hotel, I grabbed a few more shots indoors—always good to have options.

Then, I settled into work, making progress on a project video before meeting up with colleagues.

After checking into my room, I took a short break to call my kids—always the highlight of my day. Even with all the excitement of being in Berlin, nothing compares to hearing their voices.

Later in the evening, I had a quick meeting with a guest interested in AI, where we talked shop for a while. I promised to send over some useful resources, including demo videos, performance benchmarks, and details on our webinar series.

Dinner with the team was a great mix of professional conversation and casual connection. I met several new faces and enjoyed hearing different perspectives from people across the company.

The night wrapped up with a few drinks in good company before heading back to my room. Exhausted but satisfied, I crashed, ready for whatever Berlin had in store next.

Day 3 in Berlin – Thursday

A Day of Reflection, Racing, and Celebration

The day started with a classic European hotel breakfast—hard-boiled eggs, sliced meats, croissants, and coffee. Simple but satisfying. After fueling up, we hopped on the train and headed to the coworking space for the second full day of the retreat.

Morning Sessions

The morning kicked off with coffee and informal hellos—a relaxed way to ease into the day. Then came the first real session: Turning Points in Company History. It was eye-opening to see the pivotal moments that shaped the organization. A lot of things I hadn’t known before suddenly made sense.

Next, we did Personal Lifelines, an exercise where each of us mapped out the highs and lows of our lives in small groups. It was unexpectedly deep, and there was a touching moment when someone shared big personal news—everyone in the group celebrated together.

The following session focused on Company Mission, Vision & Strategy. It gave me a much clearer picture of where we are as an organization and where we’re heading. Having that kind of orientation was invaluable—it’s easy to get lost in the day-to-day, but stepping back like this made the bigger picture come into focus.

Lunch & Afternoon Work

Lunch was brought in—simple boxed salads. I went for the Asian chicken one, which was decent enough.

After lunch, we continued our deep dive into company strategy before breaking into team time with marketing. It was a productive sync, but I wished we had more than just two hours. There’s so much we could have aligned on. I also might have stirred up a little tension when I suggested implementing a project management tool—definitely got some mixed reactions.

Go-Karting Mayhem

Then came the highlight of the day: go-karting. It was an absolute blast—part Formula One, part endurance test. I was loving it until the final stretch, when pure exhaustion set in. At one point, someone bumped me while passing, and I couldn’t help but laugh—it was all in good fun and very competitive.

Evening Celebrations

After that, we headed to a street food fair for dinner. The food was excellent, and the atmosphere was buzzing. The group celebrated a big sales win, and the energy was electric—everyone was in high spirits.

Throughout the evening, I had some great, meaningful conversations with colleagues. It’s rare to have moments like that outside of work.

We wrapped up around 11 PM and made our way back to the hotel. But the night wasn’t quite over—I stayed up talking with a couple of people, learning more about their past experiences and perspectives.

Finally, at 2 AM, I crashed—completely drained but grateful for a day that felt both intense and deeply rewarding.

Day 4 in Berlin – Friday

The Last Work Day

The final workday of the retreat started with a bit of a struggle—I was definitely feeling the effects of the night before. Still, I managed to get up and meet some colleagues for breakfast before heading to Betahaus on the train.

Wrapping Up Work

The morning was filled with a few more sessions, the last push of structured work before wrapping up the retreat. By lunchtime, we split into departments for our final team meal. The marketing group went to an Asian restaurant, where I had udon with duck—absolutely delicious.

Back at Betahaus, we had a few more sessions, then the entire company gathered for a group photo. I pulled out my selfie stick and remote, prepping everything to capture the main shot.

To celebrate the end of the retreat, we enjoyed cake and champagne. I had a few glasses before heading with a group to the hotel to drop off our things.

The Final Dinner

We took the train to Café Restaurant Jolesch for our last dinner together.

The meal was fantastic—I started with soup, had traditional schnitzel as my entrée, and finished with a crème brûlée for dessert.

After dinner, we spent time outside chatting, enjoying the last moments of the retreat together. Eventually, the group split—some headed back to the hotel while the rest of us decided to keep the night going with karaoke.

Karaoke & Late-Night Adventures

Karaoke was an absolute blast. I sang a couple of favorites and teamed up with others for some energetic duets. The energy was high, and we kept the party going until about 4:30 AM.

Afterward, I grabbed a ride back to the hotel with a few people. While most called it a night, I stopped at a small restaurant for a burger and currywurst—a perfect late-night meal.

Finally, with exhaustion setting in, I headed back to the hotel and crashed hard.

Day 5 in Berlin – Saturday

Dawn of the Final Day

I woke up feeling rough—my chest hurt, my stomach hurt, and I was exhausted. The previous night had been a little too heavy on the drinks, and I was definitely paying the price. Realizing it was almost 10 and I didn’t want to miss breakfast, I got up, threw on a shirt, and headed downstairs. It was nice to say goodbye to a few people from the support team before heading back up to rest.

I slept until about 2 PM, then cleaned up, packed my bags, and caught up on a few messages and emails.

Later, I ran into a colleague who was preparing to leave, so it was good to say a proper goodbye. We even grabbed a quick selfie before parting ways.

In the evening, I went to dinner with another colleague. It was a relaxed way to close out the trip.

Now I’m in the Uber to the airport—sad that it’s over, but excited to see my kids again.

This was truly a trip for the books!

items.title: The Nest
items.summary: The Nest, Trust, and the Illusion of a Cage A nest is…
items.content_html:
The Nest, Trust, and the Illusion of a Cage

A nest is built carefully, twig by twig, with patience and intention. It is not merely a shelter—it is a home, a foundation built to protect, sustain, and nurture those within it. The nest is not a cage; it does not confine, but rather, it provides a place of belonging. It offers both security and freedom—a safe place to return to, a sanctuary that allows growth.

Birds leave the nest, but not to abandon it. They leave to gather, to experience the world, to strengthen themselves—but always with the knowledge that what they bring back will sustain and reinforce the home they share. A bird might return with food to nourish its partner, or with twigs and soft down to make the nest even stronger. Each time they venture out, they contribute to what they are building together.

In a relationship, leaving the nest should mean personal growth, exploration, and independence—but never betrayal. True partnership is not about restriction; it is about trust—the trust that each partner, when stepping away, does so with the intent to return with something of value. Whether that is wisdom, experience, support, or simply the reassurance of loyalty, the time spent outside the nest should enrich it, not weaken it.

But when one partner starts building multiple nests, dividing their energy and effort, something shifts. The twigs that should have reinforced the shared nest are instead placed elsewhere. The resources meant to sustain are spent outside, leaving what was once strong now fragile. A bird cannot nurture multiple nests with the same devotion. The more it divides itself, the weaker each nest becomes.

At first, the original nest may hold, sustained by the effort of the one who remains, but eventually, the imbalance becomes clear. The nest that once provided warmth and safety now struggles to remain whole. And if one partner gives too much outside the nest without replenishing what they have built together, the nest does not just weaken—it begins to fall apart.

Even worse, bringing predators into the nest—others who threaten the safety and integrity of what’s been built—destroys it from within. A nest thrives when it is protected, when both partners are selective about what influences they allow inside. When one bird repeatedly brings threats—whether through dishonesty, betrayal, or disregard for the shared commitment—the nest isn’t strengthened. It becomes exposed, vulnerable to being torn apart, either by outside forces or by the first storm life throws at it.

Radical acceptance teaches us that we cannot control the choices of another bird. We cannot force someone to tend to the nest if they don’t see its value. What we can do is acknowledge reality as it is, without judgment or resistance. We can accept the pain of watching twigs be plucked away, without letting that pain define our worth or our future. Acceptance is not giving up—it is choosing to respond to reality with wisdom instead of resistance.

Trust: The Invisible Threads Holding the Nest Together

Trust is the glue that holds the nest in place. It is not just about being faithful; it is about being honest, consistent, and dependable. Trust is what makes the nest feel like home. Without trust, the nest becomes fragile—no matter how well it was built, it begins to crumble, and eventually, it collapses.

Every time you tell the truth, every time you are accountable, every time you are kind and loving, you add a single twig to the nest. Over time, these twigs reinforce one another, creating something strong, stable, and lasting.

But every time you lie, betray, keep secrets, or hurt the other bird you don’t just remove a twig—you risk ripping out an entire section of the nest if it’s discovered. The damage isn’t minor; it’s catastrophic. A single dishonest moment can undo months, even years, of careful building. That’s why it’s so important to think before breaking trust—because rebuilding requires so much more effort than preserving what’s already there.

A nest isn’t just about love—it’s about consistent, thoughtful effort. Without trust, love alone is not enough to hold it together.

Radical acceptance reminds us that trust cannot be forced, only earned. We cannot demand that another bird handle the nest with care. What we can do is tend to our own integrity, ensure that our own twigs are placed with honesty and care, and accept when another bird is unwilling to do the same. And if that is the case, we must have the courage to stop waiting for them to return.

The Illusion of a Cage

Some birds look at the bottom of the nest and mistake its structure for a cage. They focus only on the boundaries—the twigs that form the edges—and feel trapped. They forget that those twigs aren’t walls keeping them in; they’re walls keeping the nest intact.

A cage is about control. A nest is about protection.

A cage is built to confine. A nest is built to nurture.

A cage forces you to stay. A nest is something you choose to return to.

The only time a nest becomes a cage is when someone tries to leave but still expects it to be there for them, unchanged, untouched, and waiting—while they build other nests elsewhere. When a bird refuses to participate in maintaining the nest but still wants to return to its warmth, it no longer sees it as a home; it sees it as an obligation or a resource.

A true partnership requires choosing the nest, not just using it when convenient. It requires recognizing that boundaries aren’t restrictions; they’re reinforcements. And the moment one partner stops respecting the nest—whether by neglect, dishonesty, or bringing outside threats into it, or hurting the other bird—the nest is no longer a safe place.

And when only one bird is fully invested in maintaining the nest, it creates an unfair burden. The bird that is still trying, still tending to the nest, feels abandoned. They are left carrying all the responsibility, waiting for a partner who only returns when it suits them.

Worse yet, the bird that once worked so hard to maintain the nest may stop, either allowing it to crumble or, in frustration, tearing out sections of the nest themselves. Resentment changes a bird—it turns effort into exhaustion, love into obligation, and warmth into distance. It’s not about one bird being right and the other being wrong—it’s about both birds giving equal effort and understanding what the effort means so that the nest remains a place of trust, not resentment.

The Consequence of Flying Without a Nest

It’s easy to believe that freedom is found in avoiding commitment altogether. A bird that never builds a nest is free to fly wherever it pleases, to land wherever it finds comfort for the moment. But without a nest, there is no safety. No stability. No peace.

A bird without a nest is at the mercy of every storm. It has no shelter when the winds pick up, no warmth when the nights grow cold. It can fly as far as it wants, but it is never truly home.

When you don’t build a nest, you don’t have to grow. You don’t have to work through discomfort, compromise, or build something lasting. You can stay the same, floating from branch to branch, without ever creating a foundation. But that also means that when you fall, there is nothing beneath you to catch you.

A nest isn’t just a place to return to. It’s a place that shapes you. It’s a place where love is tested, strengthened, and proven over time. It’s where you grow—not in isolation, but alongside the one you’ve chosen to build with.

A Well-Tended Nest: Love That Endures

A well-tended nest does not just endure—it flourishes. It becomes a sanctuary, a place of deep belonging, where two partners can return again and again, knowing they are safe in each other’s presence. It is not just a physical shelter, but an emotional and spiritual one—a home built from trust, consistency, and shared purpose.

How the Nest Protects

Life will bring storms. Hardships, losses, and struggles will come, but a strong nest shields those within it. In a well-built nest, partners do not weather the storms alone—they hold onto each other, offering comfort and reassurance through the darkest nights. They know that even when the winds rage, their commitment remains unshaken, because it was not built on fleeting emotions, but on deep, unwavering care.

Protection is not just physical safety—it is emotional safety. In a well-built nest, there is no fear of betrayal, no anxiety of being abandoned, no uncertainty about one’s worth. Each partner knows they are loved—not for what they provide, not for what they do, but for who they are. They can rest in the certainty that they are seen, known, and cherished.

How the Nest Sustains

A strong nest allows both partners to grow individually while knowing they have a steady foundation to return to. It is where love is replenished, where small acts of kindness reinforce the strength of the commitment.

It is a place where partners build each other up, where they remind each other of their strength, their dreams, and their worth. It is a place where they can be their truest selves, without masks or pretenses, and still be loved.

How the Nest Nurtures

A well-tended nest does not just sustain the couple—it extends to their children and beyond. It teaches the next generation what love looks like. It creates a legacy.

A nest built with patience and trust is not just a place for today—it is a foundation for a lifetime. It’s the place where two birds grow old together, where their wings become weaker, but their love becomes stronger. It is a nest that does not just serve them, but serves their young—offering them a foundation of love, honesty, and resilience, so they too may one day build a nest of their own.

And that is why it is worth building.

items.title: Powershell Script to convert Multiple .MD files into .CSV
items.summary: When I first started on my web design journey, I made a…
items.content_html:
When I first started on my web design journey, I made a lot of bad decisions. Thankfully, the web design world is unforgiving, and taught me early. One of these bad decisions was keeping client data stored in evernote in plain text. Over the years, I migrated over to password managers, first Lastpass, then 1Password when Lastpass got hacked.

While all my current clients were successfully migrated over, my old legacy notes still lived in Evernote. They no longer posed much of a threat, as the servers that the passwords belonged to were no longer active. As a digital data hoarder, I still didn't want to lose these data points, but I didn't have a good way to migrate them over.

Evernote outputs to a proprietary file that Joplin supports thankfully, so for a while I kept them on my Joplin instance, but as someone that is trying to reduce noise, I wanted to get this out of my journal and put it someplace more secure.

Enter ChatGPT and Powershell. I had chatgpt create a powershell script for me that took all the Markdown Files and converted them over to CSV file that I can then import into 1Password. I first created an Archive Vault for these so I also don't see them on the day to day, but can search against them if I need to.

See below:

# Initialize an empty array to hold the data
$csvData = @()

# Debug: Print the directory being scanned
Write-Host "Scanning directory: C:\Users\USER\OneDrive\Desktop\Old Business Notes"

# Loop through each .md file in the folder
Get-ChildItem -Path 'C:\Users\USER\OneDrive\Desktop\Old Business Notes' -Filter *.md | ForEach-Object {
    # Debug: Print the name of the file being processed
    Write-Host "Processing file: $($_.Name)"

    # Read the file content
    $fileContent = Get-Content $_.FullName -Raw
    
    # Debug: Print the file content
    Write-Host "File Content: $fileContent"

    # Separate the title and content
    $lines = $fileContent -split "\r?\n"
    $title = $_.BaseName  # Using the filename without extension as the title
    $content = $lines -join "`r`n"
    
    # Create an object for this file
    $obj = [PSCustomObject]@{
        "Title" = $title
        "Content" = $content
    }
    
    # Add the object to the array
    $csvData += $obj
}

# Debug: Print the CSV data to the console
Write-Host "CSV Data: $csvData"

# Export the array to CSV
$csvData | Export-Csv -Path 'C:\Users\USER\OneDrive\Desktop\Old Business Notes\output.csv' -NoTypeInformation

# Debug: Check if the file has been created
if (Test-Path 'C:\Users\USER\OneDrive\Desktop\Old Business Notes\output.csv') {
    Write-Host "CSV file created successfully."
} else {
    Write-Host "CSV file NOT created."
}

items.content_html:
This automation posts when the n8n server comes online. It also gets the amount of storage used so far and the n8n version that is currently running and adds it to the slack notification.
